phrases.translation: Alif-Lãm-Mĩm-Ṣãd
phrases.explanation: These are the separate letters recited at the opening of the surah. The text does not explain their full meaning, so readers should avoid claiming certainty about them. Their presence invites attentive reading of the revelation that follows.

phrases.translation: ˹This is˺ a Book sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺—
phrases.explanation: The Qur’an is presented as a Book sent down to the Prophet. This opening establishes revelation as the source of the message, rather than personal invention, and introduces the guidance discussed throughout the surah.

phrases.translation: do not let anxiety into your heart regarding it—
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told not to let anxiety about the Book weigh on his heart. The reassurance acknowledges the strain of conveying a message that some listeners reject, while strengthening him to continue.

phrases.translation: so with it you may warn ˹the disbelievers˺,
phrases.explanation: The Book is given so the Prophet can warn those who disbelieve. A warning makes consequences clear before they arrive, giving people an opportunity to reconsider their choices and respond.

phrases.translation: and as a reminder to the believers
phrases.explanation: The Qur’an is also a reminder for believers. It renews their awareness of Allah and helps them remain steady in faith, so the same revelation can warn one audience and strengthen another.

phrases.translation: Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord,
phrases.explanation: People are instructed to follow what has been sent down from their Lord. The verse places revealed guidance above personal preference and calls for a response in belief and conduct.

phrases.translation: and do not take others as guardians besides Him.
phrases.explanation: Believers should not take other guardians besides Allah. The warning concerns giving others the ultimate loyalty and authority that belong to God, not seeking ordinary help or cooperating with people.

phrases.translation: How seldom are you mindful
phrases.explanation: The question asks how seldom people are mindful. It turns the command into a moment of self-examination, urging listeners to notice how easily distraction weakens their attention to guidance in daily life.

phrases.translation: ˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed!
phrases.explanation: The audience is asked to imagine how many societies were destroyed. Their fate serves as a warning that communities can lose their security when they persist in rejecting guidance and doing wrong.

phrases.translation: Our torment took them by surprise ˹while sleeping˺ at night or midday
phrases.explanation: The torment came by surprise at night or midday, including while people slept. The timing emphasizes how little control they had over its arrival and urges the living not to assume consequences will wait.

phrases.translation: Their only cry—when overwhelmed by Our torment—was,
phrases.explanation: When the torment overwhelmed them, the people had no elaborate defense or excuse. Their only response was an admission of wrongdoing, showing how clear their guilt appeared when the consequences arrived.

phrases.translation: “We have indeed been wrongdoers.”
phrases.explanation: They confess, “We have indeed been wrongdoers.” The admission confirms that they recognize their actions as unjust, but it comes after destruction has begun, when repentance can no longer change the outcome.

phrases.translation: We will surely question those who received messengers
phrases.explanation: Those who received messengers will be questioned. The verse presents revelation as creating responsibility: people are asked how they responded after guidance was delivered to them and what they did with it in their lives.

phrases.translation: and We will question the messengers ˹themselves˺
phrases.explanation: The messengers themselves will also be questioned. Their mission and testimony are part of the final account, which examines both the people addressed and those entrusted to convey the message.

phrases.translation: Then We will give them a full account with sure knowledge—
phrases.explanation: Allah will give a full account with sure knowledge. Nothing in the record depends on rumor or incomplete human memory, since the judgment is based on knowledge of what truly occurred.

phrases.translation: for We were never absent
phrases.explanation: Allah was never absent from what people did. The verse grounds the certainty of the account in divine presence and awareness, so no action or response to guidance has escaped His knowledge.

phrases.translation: The weighing on that Day will be just.
phrases.explanation: The weighing on the Day of Judgment will be just. No one will be assessed unfairly or by unreliable appearances. The verse assures people that the final evaluation is governed by perfect justice.

phrases.translation: As for those whose scale will be heavy ˹with good deeds˺,
phrases.explanation: A heavy scale represents a weight of good deeds in the final reckoning. The image directs attention to the moral value of a person’s actions, not to social standing or worldly possessions.

phrases.translation: ˹only˺ they will be successful
phrases.explanation: Those whose scale is heavy will be successful. The verse defines lasting success by the outcome of judgment, inviting people to value goodness and faithfulness over temporary recognition in the final reckoning.

phrases.translation: But those whose scale is light,
phrases.explanation: A light scale describes a person whose good deeds do not outweigh their wrongdoing. The contrast with the previous verse makes the final judgment a serious measure of how people lived.

phrases.translation: they have doomed themselves
phrases.explanation: Those people have doomed themselves. Their loss is the result of their own choices, not an injustice imposed on them, and the verse calls readers to take responsibility before judgment.

phrases.translation: for wrongfully denying Our signs
phrases.explanation: They wrongfully denied Allah’s signs. The verse connects their outcome with rejecting revealed guidance, warning that denial can lead people to harm their own prospects in the Hereafter when faced with clear evidence.

phrases.translation: We have indeed established you on earth
phrases.explanation: Allah established people on earth, giving humanity a place to live and act. The verse presents life in the world as a provision and responsibility, not an achievement independent of the Creator.

phrases.translation: and provided you with a means of livelihood.
phrases.explanation: People have been provided with means of livelihood. Food, work, and other necessities are gifts that support daily life, and recognizing their source can deepen gratitude and responsible use in everyday life.

phrases.translation: ˹Yet˺ you seldom give any thanks
phrases.explanation: Despite these provisions, people seldom give thanks. The closing challenges forgetfulness: enjoying the earth and its resources should lead to recognition of Allah and care in how those gifts are used.

phrases.translation: Surely We created you,
phrases.explanation: Allah says that He created humanity. The statement establishes dependence on the Creator before recounting the story of Adam, placing human dignity and responsibility within that relationship from the beginning.

phrases.translation: then shaped you,
phrases.explanation: Human beings were then shaped. The verse describes creation as deliberate, preparing for the account of Adam and the command that tests Iblis’s humility and obedience to Allah rather than pride.

phrases.translation: then said to the angels,
phrases.explanation: After creating and shaping humanity, Allah addressed the angels. The command that follows marks a decisive moment in the story, revealing whether each being would obey or resist Allah’s authority in the moment.

phrases.translation: “Prostrate before Adam,”
phrases.explanation: The angels are commanded to prostrate before Adam. In this account, their act is obedience to Allah’s command and an honor granted to Adam, not worship of a human being.

phrases.translation: so they all did—but not Iblîs,
phrases.explanation: The others obey, but Iblis refuses. His exception introduces the conflict that drives the following verses and shows that being present for a command does not guarantee humility or obedience.

phrases.translation: who refused to prostrate with the others
phrases.explanation: Iblis refused to prostrate with the others. The refusal is presented as a deliberate rejection of Allah’s command, setting up his explanation and the arrogance that is condemned in the next verse.

phrases.translation: Allah asked, “What prevented you from prostrating
phrases.explanation: Allah asks Iblis what prevented him from prostrating. The question gives him a chance to explain his refusal, while making clear that the command came directly from Allah and expected obedience.

phrases.translation: when I commanded you?”
phrases.explanation: The question stresses that Iblis was commanded. His refusal was not a misunderstanding of what Allah wanted, but a choice to resist an instruction he had clearly received and understood.

phrases.translation: He replied, “I am better than he is:
phrases.explanation: Iblis claims superiority over Adam. The statement reveals pride: instead of obeying, he judges another creature’s worth and treats his own comparison as a reason to reject Allah’s clear command.

phrases.translation: You created me from fire and him from clay.”
phrases.explanation: Iblis contrasts his creation from fire with Adam’s from clay. He assumes one material makes him superior, but the verse shows that this reasoning cannot justify disobedience or arrogance in Allah’s sight.

phrases.translation: Allah said, “Then get down from Paradise!
phrases.explanation: Allah orders Iblis to descend from Paradise. His refusal and pride have consequences, and the command marks his loss of a place he had occupied among those addressed in the divine command.

phrases.translation: It is not for you to be arrogant here.
phrases.explanation: Paradise is not a place for Iblis to act arrogantly. The verse treats pride as incompatible with obedience and reminds readers that status cannot excuse defiance of Allah or a claim of rank.

phrases.translation: So get out!
phrases.explanation: The command to leave is repeated emphatically. Iblis is not invited to remain after rejecting the order, and the repetition underscores the seriousness of his deliberate rebellion and makes the sentence unmistakable.

phrases.translation: You are truly one of the disgraced.”
phrases.explanation: Iblis is counted among the disgraced. His humiliation follows from pride and refusal, warning that a claim of superiority does not protect anyone from the consequences of disobedience before his Lord.

phrases.translation: He appealed, “Then delay my end
phrases.explanation: Iblis appeals for his end to be delayed. Rather than ask forgiveness for refusing Allah’s command, he asks to remain until a later time, revealing that his response is still not repentance.

phrases.translation: until the Day of their resurrection.”
phrases.explanation: He asks for delay until the Day of resurrection. The request sets the time frame for his later effort to mislead people, which he describes in the following verses of the story.

phrases.translation: Allah said, “You are delayed
phrases.explanation: Allah grants Iblis a delay. The response allows the conflict described in the next verses to unfold, but it does not mean Allah approves of Iblis’s rebellion or future temptation.

phrases.translation: ˹until the appointed Day˺.”
phrases.explanation: The delay lasts until the appointed Day. Its limit is set by Allah, showing that Iblis’s time is not independent or endless, even as he plans to mislead people beyond that appointed limit.

phrases.translation: He said, “For leaving me to stray
phrases.explanation: Iblis blames Allah for leaving him to stray. The statement shifts responsibility away from his own refusal, illustrating how pride can turn into accusation instead of honest repentance or admitting his choice.

phrases.translation: I will lie in ambush for them on Your Straight Path
phrases.explanation: Iblis vows to lie in ambush for people on Allah’s Straight Path. His target is those seeking guidance, so the verse warns that temptation can challenge believers precisely as they try to do right.

phrases.translation: I will approach them from their front,
phrases.explanation: Iblis says he will approach people from the front. The list begins to describe an all-sided effort to mislead, suggesting that temptation can meet people as they move toward what lies ahead.

phrases.translation: their back,
phrases.explanation: He also names their back, adding another direction to his threat. The wording presents no part of a person’s journey as free from challenge, so vigilance is needed throughout life.

phrases.translation: their right, their left,
phrases.explanation: Iblis includes both the right and left in his plan. The repeated directions convey persistence from every side, rather than a map of specific physical approaches or a claim that any direction is evil.

phrases.translation: and then You will find most of them ungrateful.”
phrases.explanation: Iblis expects most people to be ungrateful. The verse portrays ingratitude as one result of temptation, urging people to remember Allah and resist the pride that began this story in everyday decisions.

phrases.translation: Allah said, “Get out of Paradise!
phrases.explanation: Allah orders Iblis to leave Paradise. The command confirms that the earlier delay is not permission to remain there or to continue his disobedience without consequences, as Allah has set a time for him.

phrases.translation: You are disgraced and rejected!
phrases.explanation: Iblis is described as disgraced and rejected. His position follows from deliberate arrogance, and the words warn against treating rebellion as a path to lasting honor or respect in Allah’s judgment.

phrases.translation: I will certainly fill up Hell with you and your followers all together.”
phrases.explanation: Allah says Hell will be filled with Iblis and his followers together. The warning presents the end of persistent rebellion and invites people not to follow the path of deception.

phrases.translation: ˹Allah said,˺ “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat from wherever you please,
phrases.explanation: Adam and his wife are invited to live in Paradise and eat freely from its provisions. The broad permission highlights abundance, with the single restriction that follows setting a clear boundary.

phrases.translation: but do not approach this tree,
phrases.explanation: They are told not to approach one particular tree. The command is specific, so the test is not a denial of all provision but a call to respect a boundary set by Allah.

phrases.translation: or else you will be wrongdoers.”
phrases.explanation: Crossing that boundary would make them wrongdoers. The warning is given before the temptation in the next verse, showing that Adam and his wife know the instruction they are being asked to keep.

phrases.translation: Then Satan tempted them in order to expose what was hidden of their nakedness.
phrases.explanation: Satan tempts Adam and his wife with the aim of exposing what was hidden of their nakedness. The verse portrays temptation as an effort to lead them into disobedience and vulnerability.

phrases.translation: He said, “Your Lord has forbidden this tree to you only to prevent you from becoming angels or immortals.”
phrases.explanation: Satan claims the tree was forbidden only to prevent them from becoming angels or immortals. His words offer a flattering motive for doubt, illustrating how temptation can recast a clear limit as unfair deprivation.

phrases.translation: And he swore to them, “I am truly your sincere advisor.”
phrases.explanation: Satan swears that he is a sincere adviser to Adam and his wife. The claim sounds caring, but it is a lie designed to make them trust him, showing how temptation can disguise itself as concern.

phrases.translation: So he brought about their fall through deception.
phrases.explanation: Satan brings about their fall by deceiving them. His success depends on misleading their judgment, and the verse warns that a trusted-sounding claim can still draw people away from a clear command.

phrases.translation: And when they tasted of the tree,
phrases.explanation: Adam and his wife taste the tree after Satan’s deception. Their action crosses the boundary Allah had set, and the events that follow show the consequence of that choice and its consequences.

phrases.translation: their nakedness was exposed to them, prompting them to cover themselves with leaves from Paradise.
phrases.explanation: Their nakedness becomes exposed, so they cover themselves with leaves from Paradise. The scene presents an immediate awareness of vulnerability after disobedience and the instinctive attempt to respond to it.

phrases.translation: Then their Lord called out to them,
phrases.explanation: Their Lord calls out to them after they disobey. The question that follows reminds them of the instruction they received and gives them a chance to face what happened honestly.

phrases.translation: “Did I not forbid you from that tree
phrases.explanation: Allah asks whether He had not forbidden them from the tree. The question recalls that the boundary was explicit, so their act cannot be explained as ignorance of the command.

phrases.translation: and ˹did I not˺ tell you that Satan is your sworn enemy?”
phrases.explanation: Allah had also warned them that Satan was their sworn enemy. The reminder exposes the deception they trusted and teaches readers to be wary of an adversary who presents himself as a friend.

phrases.translation: They replied, “Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves.
phrases.explanation: Adam and his wife acknowledge that they wronged themselves. Their words accept responsibility instead of blaming Satan or denying the command, making this confession a model of honest recognition and repentance.

phrases.translation: If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us,
phrases.explanation: They ask Allah for forgiveness and mercy. The request recognizes that wrongdoing needs both pardon and divine compassion, and that they cannot repair the relationship by relying on their own power alone.

phrases.translation: we will certainly be losers.”
phrases.explanation: They say they would be among the losers without forgiveness and mercy. The confession shows that hope depends on Allah’s compassion and that turning back begins with acknowledging one’s need.

phrases.translation: Allah said, “Descend as enemies to each other.
phrases.explanation: Allah tells them to descend as enemies to one another. The story moves from life in Paradise to a world marked by conflict, where people must navigate the consequences of disobedience.

phrases.translation: You will find in the earth a residence and provision
phrases.explanation: The earth will provide a residence and sustenance for them. Human life on earth is presented as a temporary stage with real needs, but not as an existence independent of Allah.

phrases.translation: for your appointed stay.”
phrases.explanation: Their stay on earth has an appointed term. The verse places human life within a limit, preparing for the next statement that people will live, die, and be resurrected in due course.

phrases.translation: He added, “There you will live,
phrases.explanation: People will live on earth. The statement marks ordinary human life as part of the sequence that began with Adam’s descent, giving each generation a period in which to choose how to respond to guidance.

phrases.translation: there you will die,
phrases.explanation: They will also die on earth. The reminder keeps worldly life in perspective: residence and provision are temporary, and death is not the final end of human existence for any generation.

phrases.translation: and from there you will be resurrected.”
phrases.explanation: From the earth people will be resurrected. The verse affirms life after death, connecting humanity’s beginning and return to the earth with the coming resurrection, judgment, and accountability that follows.

phrases.translation: O children of Adam!
phrases.explanation: The address speaks to all children of Adam, carrying the lesson beyond the first couple. The commands that follow concern human dignity and the way believers prepare for worship in the world.

phrases.translation: We have provided for you clothing to cover your nakedness and as an adornment.
phrases.explanation: Allah provides clothing to cover nakedness and as adornment. The verse recognizes both modesty and beauty as part of human life, presenting clothing as a provision rather than something to despise.

phrases.translation: However, the best clothing is righteousness.
phrases.explanation: Righteousness is described as the best clothing. The image extends beyond fabric to inward moral character, suggesting that outward dress is not a substitute for reverence, humility, and good conduct.

phrases.translation: This is one of Allah’s bounties,
phrases.explanation: Clothing and the reminder about righteousness are among Allah’s bounties. The verse directs attention from material provision to moral guidance, both of which deserve gratitude and sustain physical and spiritual life.

phrases.translation: so perhaps you will be mindful
phrases.explanation: The purpose is that people may be mindful. Awareness of Allah should shape both outward choices and inner conduct, helping believers treat clothing, worship, and modesty as parts of a thoughtful life.

phrases.translation: O children of Adam! Do not let Satan deceive you
phrases.explanation: The children of Adam are warned not to let Satan deceive them as he deceived their parents. Recalling Adam and his wife makes the danger personal and shows that temptation continues across generations.

phrases.translation: as he tempted your parents out of Paradise and caused their cover to be removed in order to expose their nakedness.
phrases.explanation: Satan’s temptation led Adam and his wife to lose their covering and expose their nakedness. The verse recalls the cost of disobedience and urges later people not to repeat the mistake.

phrases.translation: Surely he and his soldiers watch you from where you cannot see them.
phrases.explanation: Satan and his soldiers can see people from where people cannot see them. The warning evokes an unseen spiritual threat and calls for vigilance rather than confidence that temptation is always obvious.

phrases.translation: We have made the devils allies of those who disbelieve
phrases.explanation: The verse says devils have been made allies of those who disbelieve. It describes a relationship of shared opposition to guidance, not a reason to treat every individual who disagrees as an enemy.

phrases.translation: Whenever they commit a shameful deed,
phrases.explanation: When people commit a shameful deed, the verse turns to the excuses they offer. The example warns that repeating a harmful practice does not make it morally sound or divinely approved.

phrases.translation: they say, “We found our forefathers doing it
phrases.explanation: They appeal to the example of their forefathers. Inherited custom can explain how a practice began, but it does not by itself prove that the practice is right or binding for all time.

phrases.translation: and Allah has commanded us to do it.”
phrases.explanation: They go further and claim that Allah commanded the shameful act. The verse challenges this false attribution, since tradition cannot be turned into revelation without clear, direct evidence from Allah.

phrases.translation: Say, “No! Allah never commands what is shameful.
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to answer that Allah never commands what is shameful. The reply rejects using God’s name to excuse wrongdoing and calls people to distinguish revelation from invention.

phrases.translation: How can you attribute to Allah what you do not know?”
phrases.explanation: The final question asks how people can attribute to Allah what they do not know. It warns against speaking for God without knowledge, a principle that applies to religious claims and everyday judgment.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “My Lord has commanded uprightness
phrases.explanation: Allah commands uprightness. The instruction calls people to justice and sound conduct, contrasting with the shameful practices and false religious claims rejected in the previous verse and in their dealings with others.

phrases.translation: and dedication ˹to Him alone˺ in worship,
phrases.explanation: Worship is to be dedicated to Allah alone. Sincere devotion rejects showing off or turning religious practice into a means of gaining status or praise from other people in the community.

phrases.translation: calling upon Him with sincere devotion.
phrases.explanation: People are told to call upon Allah with sincere devotion. The verse links prayer with a heart directed to God, rather than a performance shaped for an audience, whether alone or in public.

phrases.translation: Just as He first brought you into being, you will be brought to life again.”
phrases.explanation: Just as Allah first brought people into being, He will bring them to life again. The reminder connects creation with resurrection and gives present choices significance beyond worldly life and judgment.

phrases.translation: He has guided some, while others are destined to stray.
phrases.explanation: Some people are guided while others are destined to stray. The verse recognizes different outcomes, and the next phrase describes how choosing devils as allies marks a path away from Allah.

phrases.translation: They have taken devils as their masters instead of Allah—
phrases.explanation: Those who stray take devils as their masters instead of Allah. The verse describes misplaced loyalty and spiritual authority, setting false guides against the guidance that comes from God and revelation.

phrases.translation: thinking they are ˹rightly˺ guided
phrases.explanation: They imagine that they are rightly guided. The warning is that confidence does not prove a path is sound. People need to test their choices against revelation rather than self-assurance alone.

phrases.translation: O Children of Adam! Dress properly whenever you are at worship.
phrases.explanation: The children of Adam are told to dress properly when they worship. The instruction treats preparation for worship as part of reverence and connects clothing with the earlier reminder about modesty.

phrases.translation: Eat and drink, but do not waste.
phrases.explanation: People may eat and drink, but should not waste. The verse balances enjoyment of provision with restraint, rejecting both needless excess and the idea that gratitude requires refusing lawful food.

phrases.translation: Surely He does not like the wasteful
phrases.explanation: Allah does not like the wasteful. The closing turns moderation into a matter of character, encouraging believers to use resources responsibly, remember their source, and avoid excess in consumption in daily life.

phrases.translation: Ask, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Who has forbidden the adornments and lawful provisions Allah has brought forth for His servants?”
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to ask who forbade the adornments and good provisions Allah made. The question challenges people who turn their preferences into restrictions without authority from revelation or divine command.

phrases.translation: Say, “They are for the enjoyment of the believers in this worldly life,
phrases.explanation: These provisions are for believers to enjoy in worldly life. The verse presents lawful beauty and sustenance as gifts, not as things that faith requires people to reject or view as spiritually wrong.

phrases.translation: but they will be exclusively theirs on the Day of Judgment.
phrases.explanation: The believers will have these blessings exclusively on the Day of Judgment. The contrast distinguishes the temporary sharing of worldly provision from the lasting reward promised in the Hereafter after this present life.

phrases.translation: This is how We make Our revelations clear for people
phrases.explanation: Allah makes His revelations clear. The explanation of lawful enjoyment and future reward is meant to be understood rather than replaced by unsupported prohibitions or guesswork about revelation, with careful reflection.

phrases.translation: of knowledge.”
phrases.explanation: The signs are made clear for people of knowledge. Knowledge helps people distinguish what Allah permits from rules invented without proof, and encourages thoughtful gratitude rather than superstition about His provisions.

phrases.translation: Say, “My Lord has only forbidden open and secret indecencies, sinfulness, unjust aggression,
phrases.explanation: Allah forbids open and hidden indecencies, sin, and unjust aggression. The list moves from personal wrongdoing to harm against others, showing that faith includes both private morality and public justice.

phrases.translation: associating ˹others˺ with Allah ˹in worship˺—a practice He has never authorized—and
phrases.explanation: Associating partners with Allah is forbidden, and the verse stresses that He never authorized it. The wording rejects the attempt to give idolatry religious legitimacy or assign divine authority to others.

phrases.translation: attributing to Allah what you do not know.”
phrases.explanation: The final prohibition is attributing to Allah what people do not know. The verse warns against fabricating religious rules or claims, since speaking without knowledge can mislead others and distort worship.

phrases.translation: For each community there is an appointed term.
phrases.explanation: Each community has an appointed term. The verse presents the life of societies as limited, placing historical power within a larger order determined by Allah and His decree, not by human control.

phrases.translation: When their time arrives,
phrases.explanation: When a community’s time arrives, the moment of consequence has come. The statement cautions against assuming that a society can postpone its appointed reckoning indefinitely and should prompt reflection about its conduct.

phrases.translation: they can neither delay it for a moment, nor could they advance it
phrases.explanation: No one can delay or advance that term even briefly. The verse stresses the certainty of the appointed time and encourages people to respond to guidance before it arrives, without fail.

phrases.translation: O children of Adam! When messengers from among yourselves come to you reciting My revelations—
phrases.explanation: Messengers from among the children of Adam come reciting Allah’s revelations. The address recalls the repeated sending of guidance and makes clear that people are not left without a message.

phrases.translation: whoever shuns evil
phrases.explanation: Whoever shuns evil is described as responding well to the messengers. Avoiding wrongdoing is the first part of the response, not merely hearing the revelations and acknowledging the message without acting on it.

phrases.translation: and mends their ways,
phrases.explanation: Mending one’s ways means correcting conduct after recognizing evil. The verse pairs moral reform with avoidance, showing that a person can turn away from past wrongs and choose better actions.

phrases.translation: there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve
phrases.explanation: Those who respond in this way will have no fear and will not grieve. The promise offers reassurance to people who follow the message and work to change their conduct.

phrases.translation: But those who receive Our revelations with denial and arrogance will be the residents of the Fire.
phrases.explanation: Those who deny Allah’s revelations and meet them arrogantly are described as residents of the Fire. The verse warns against rejecting guidance with pride, not against honest questions or efforts to understand.

phrases.translation: They will be there forever
phrases.explanation: The verse says they will remain there forever. Its severe warning emphasizes the gravity of persistent denial and arrogance toward revelation. The next verse describes the final account that follows such rejection.

phrases.translation: Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His revelations?
phrases.explanation: The verse asks who could do more wrong than those who invent lies about Allah or deny His revelations. It identifies false religious authority and deliberate rejection as serious injustices.

phrases.translation: They will receive what is destined for them, until Our messenger-angels arrive to take their souls,
phrases.explanation: The wrongdoers receive what is destined for them until messenger-angels arrive to take their souls. The scene depicts death as the point at which worldly excuses give way to accountability.

phrases.translation: asking them, “Where are those ˹false gods˺ you used to invoke besides Allah?”
phrases.explanation: The angels ask where the false gods are that the people invoked besides Allah. The question exposes the absence of the protection and help those objects of worship were expected to provide.

phrases.translation: They will cry, “They have failed us,”
phrases.explanation: The people admit that their false gods have failed them. Their confession reveals that the beings they relied on cannot rescue them at the moment of judgment, when they need help most.

phrases.translation: and they will confess against themselves that they were indeed disbelievers
phrases.explanation: They also confess against themselves that they were disbelievers. The verse shows that their own admission confirms their rejection, leaving no basis to blame the outcome on ignorance or injustice.

phrases.translation: Allah will say, “Enter the Fire along with the ˹evil˺ groups of jinn and humans that preceded you.”
phrases.explanation: Allah orders the wrongdoers to enter the Fire with earlier groups of jinn and humans. The statement places each generation within a history of choices and consequences, not outside divine judgment.

phrases.translation: Whenever a group enters Hell,
phrases.explanation: Whenever a group enters Hell, the next part of the verse describes its response to those who went before. The scene presents a chain of blame among people who shared wrongdoing.

phrases.translation: it will curse the preceding one
phrases.explanation: Each group curses the one that preceded it. The hostility continues even after judgment, as followers and leaders accuse one another rather than finding a way to escape the outcome.

phrases.translation: until they are all gathered inside,
phrases.explanation: All the groups are gathered inside before the followers speak about their leaders. The sequence makes clear that no one can avoid judgment simply by blaming another party for their choices or actions.

phrases.translation: the followers will say about their leaders, “Our Lord! They have misled us, so multiply their torment in the Fire.”
phrases.explanation: The followers say their leaders misled them and ask for multiplied torment. The plea shows that influence creates anger and a desire to shift blame, but does not remove personal responsibility.

phrases.translation: He will answer, “It has already been multiplied for all, but you do not know.”
phrases.explanation: Allah answers that the torment is multiplied for all, while they do not know. The reply rejects the idea that one group’s blame can settle the matter and emphasizes that each is accountable, while their full fate remains beyond their understanding.

phrases.translation: Then the leaders will say to their followers, “You were no better than us!
phrases.explanation: The leaders tell their followers that they were no better than them. The exchange exposes the futility of expecting status or leadership to shield anyone from the consequences of shared wrongdoing.

phrases.translation: So taste the torment
phrases.explanation: The leaders tell the followers to taste the torment. Their words offer no rescue or apology, only confirmation that those who followed them share responsibility for what they committed before Allah.

phrases.translation: for what you used to commit.”
phrases.explanation: The punishment is tied to what they used to do. The verse emphasizes the connection between conduct and consequence, rather than treating judgment as arbitrary or unrelated to people’s actions.

phrases.translation: Surely those who receive our revelations with denial and arrogance,
phrases.explanation: The verse describes people who receive Allah’s revelations with both denial and arrogance. Their problem is not merely lack of information but a proud refusal to accept the guidance they encounter.

phrases.translation: the gates of heaven will not be opened for them,
phrases.explanation: The gates of heaven will not be opened for them. The image conveys exclusion from the way to divine acceptance and underscores the consequences of persistent denial and arrogance toward revelation.

phrases.translation: nor will they enter Paradise until a camel passes through the eye of a needle.
phrases.explanation: Their entry into Paradise is compared to a camel passing through a needle’s eye, an image of impossibility. The comparison emphasizes how incompatible their arrogance and rejection are with that reward.

phrases.translation: This is how We reward the wicked
phrases.explanation: This is how Allah rewards the wicked. The verse concludes with a warning about the consequence of denying revelation arrogantly, encouraging humility and a serious response to guidance before judgment.

phrases.translation: Hell will be their bed;
phrases.explanation: Hell is described as the wrongdoers’ bed. The image conveys that punishment will surround them rather than offer rest, reversing the comfort people ordinarily expect from a bed in worldly life.

phrases.translation: flames will be their cover.
phrases.explanation: Flames are described as their cover. The paired images of bed and covering emphasize that they cannot escape the consequences of wrongdoing or find shelter from them, even in death.

phrases.translation: This is how We reward the wrongdoers
phrases.explanation: This is how the wrongdoers are rewarded. The wording connects the outcome to their actions, presenting judgment as a consequence of persistent wrongdoing rather than an arbitrary event imposed without cause.

phrases.translation: As for those who believe and do good—
phrases.explanation: The verse turns to people who believe and do good. Faith is paired with action, so the promise concerns not only what people profess but also how they live and practice their faith.

phrases.translation: We never require of any soul more than what it can afford—
phrases.explanation: Allah does not require a soul beyond what it can afford. This reassurance places the call to good deeds within human capacity and rejects the idea that sincere believers must achieve the impossible.

phrases.translation: it is they who will be the residents of Paradise.
phrases.explanation: Those who believe and act well will be residents of Paradise. The promise offers hope after the previous warning and makes the final outcome depend on faith and good conduct.

phrases.translation: They will be there forever
phrases.explanation: They will remain there forever. The contrast with temporary earthly life emphasizes that Paradise is lasting, while the actions and choices made in life have consequences beyond death and the grave.

phrases.translation: We will remove whatever bitterness they had in their hearts.
phrases.explanation: Allah removes bitterness from the hearts of Paradise’s residents. The description portrays the Hereafter as a place where resentment and hostility no longer burden people who have been granted peace.

phrases.translation: Rivers will flow under their feet.
phrases.explanation: Rivers flow beneath their feet, adding to the image of comfort and abundance. The verse describes Paradise through familiar signs of life and provision, now enjoyed without worldly hardship or scarcity.

phrases.translation: And they will say, “Praise be to Allah for guiding us to this.
phrases.explanation: The residents praise Allah for guiding them to this reward. Their first response to Paradise is gratitude, recognizing that reaching it depended on divine guidance rather than their own strength alone.

phrases.translation: We would have never been guided if Allah had not guided us.
phrases.explanation: They acknowledge that they would not have been guided if Allah had not guided them. The words combine personal recognition with humility about the divine help that made their faith possible.

phrases.translation: The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth.”
phrases.explanation: They affirm that their Lord’s messengers truly brought the message. The statement confirms the truth of revelation after its promised outcome has become clear, vindicating the messengers’ warnings to their people.

phrases.translation: It will be announced to them, “This is Paradise awarded to you for what you used to do.”
phrases.explanation: Paradise is announced as a reward for what they used to do. The verse joins gratitude for guidance with recognition that their actions mattered in the path that led to this home.

phrases.translation: The residents of Paradise will call out to the residents of the Fire, “We have certainly found our Lord’s promise to be true.
phrases.explanation: The residents of Paradise say they found their Lord’s promise to be true. Their experience confirms the reliability of revelation and contrasts with the doubts or denials that characterized worldly life.

phrases.translation: Have you too found your Lord’s promise to be true?”
phrases.explanation: They ask the residents of the Fire whether they too found the promise true. The question highlights the different outcomes while showing that the warning and promise were both fulfilled.

phrases.translation: They will reply, “Yes, we have!”
phrases.explanation: The residents of the Fire answer yes. Their admission confirms that the promise was real, but recognition after judgment cannot undo choices made when they had a chance to respond during worldly life.

phrases.translation: Then a caller will announce to both, “May Allah’s condemnation be upon the wrongdoers
phrases.explanation: A caller announces Allah’s condemnation upon the wrongdoers. The statement is followed by a description of their conduct, showing that the judgment concerns people who actively obstructed guidance and denied the Hereafter.

phrases.translation: those who hindered ˹others˺ from Allah’s Way,
phrases.explanation: The wrongdoers hindered others from Allah’s Way. Their wrongdoing affected more than themselves because they tried to prevent others in their communities from finding and following guidance. The verse shows how obstruction can harm entire groups.

phrases.translation: strived to make it ˹appear˺ crooked,
phrases.explanation: They tried to make Allah’s Way appear crooked. The phrase describes deliberate distortion of guidance, encouraging readers to distinguish honest discussion from efforts to make the teaching seem false or unjust.

phrases.translation: and disbelieved in the Hereafter.”
phrases.explanation: They also disbelieved in the Hereafter. The list links obstruction, distortion, and denial of accountability, warning that rejection can become an active campaign against guidance and a source of further harm.

phrases.translation: There will be a barrier between Paradise and Hell.
phrases.explanation: A barrier separates Paradise and Hell. The verse then introduces people on the heights of that barrier, placing them in a position from which they can recognize both groups and their distinct outcomes.

phrases.translation: And on the heights ˹of that barrier˺ will be people who will recognize ˹the residents of˺ both by their appearance.
phrases.explanation: The people on the heights recognize the residents of Paradise and the Fire by their appearance. The scene presents them as witnesses to the distinct outcomes of the two groups.

phrases.translation: They will call out to the residents of Paradise, “Peace be upon you!”
phrases.explanation: They call out peace to the residents of Paradise. Their greeting expresses goodwill toward those who have received safety, even as the callers themselves have not yet entered, and serves as a blessing.

phrases.translation: They will have not yet entered Paradise, but eagerly hope to
phrases.explanation: They have not yet entered Paradise, but eagerly hope to do so. The line holds hope alongside uncertainty and shows their longing for the safety and welcome granted to its residents.

phrases.translation: When their eyes will turn towards the residents of Hell, they will pray, “Our Lord! Do not join us with the wrongdoing people.”
phrases.explanation: When the people on the heights look toward the Fire, they ask Allah not to join them with the wrongdoers. The prayer expresses fear of judgment and dependence on divine protection.

phrases.translation: Those on the heights will call out to some ˹tyrants in the Fire˺, who they will recognize by their appearance,
phrases.explanation: Those on the heights call out to some tyrants whom they recognize by appearance. The scene shows worldly power and reputation exposed in the Hereafter, where former status cannot shield anyone.

phrases.translation: saying, “Your large numbers and arrogance are of no use ˹today˺
phrases.explanation: They tell the tyrants that their large numbers and arrogance are of no use today. The verse contrasts worldly confidence with the helplessness of those facing judgment, who can no longer rely on earthly prestige.

phrases.translation: Are these ˹humble believers˺ the ones you swore would never be shown Allah’s mercy?”
phrases.explanation: The people on the heights ask whether the humble believers were the ones the tyrants swore would never receive Allah’s mercy. The question exposes the arrogance of those who presumed to decide whom God would favor.

phrases.translation: ˹Finally, those on the heights will be told:˺ “Enter Paradise!
phrases.explanation: The humble believers are finally told to enter Paradise. Their welcome overturns the tyrants’ earlier claim that these people would never receive mercy, showing that human predictions cannot limit Allah’s generosity.

phrases.translation: There will be no fear for you, nor will you grieve.”
phrases.explanation: They will have no fear and will not grieve. The promise describes lasting safety in Paradise, contrasting with the fear and uncertainty experienced by those still facing judgment and its consequences.

phrases.translation: The residents of the Fire will then cry out to the residents of Paradise,
phrases.explanation: The residents of the Fire call to those in Paradise for help. The scene reverses the comfort and security of the two groups, showing that worldly access to wealth cannot secure provision in the Hereafter.

phrases.translation: “Aid us with some water or any provision Allah has granted you.”
phrases.explanation: They ask for water or any provision Allah has granted the residents of Paradise. The request reveals their need, while the answer that follows describes their exclusion from these blessings.

phrases.translation: They will reply, “Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers
phrases.explanation: The residents of Paradise reply that Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers. The exchange presents the Fire as a place without access to the provisions enjoyed by the people of Paradise.

phrases.translation: those who took this faith ˹of Islam˺ as mere amusement and play
phrases.explanation: The verse describes people who treated the faith as amusement and play. It criticizes dismissing religious responsibility as a joke or treating the message carelessly, rather than addressing honest questions or thoughtful disagreement.

phrases.translation: and were deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life.”
phrases.explanation: They were deluded by worldly life. The verse warns that immediate pleasures can distract people from accountability and make a serious message seem unimportant, until they forget death and judgment.

phrases.translation: ˹Allah will say,˺ “Today We will ignore them just as they ignored the coming of this Day of theirs
phrases.explanation: Allah says He will ignore them as they ignored the coming of this Day. The parallel emphasizes the consequences of dismissing accountability when guidance was available and rejecting the reminder during life.

phrases.translation: and for rejecting Our revelations.”
phrases.explanation: They are also judged for rejecting Allah’s revelations. The verse links their neglect of the Hereafter with turning away from guidance, while the earlier parts of the passage explain that a Book was sent to warn them.

phrases.translation: We have certainly brought them a Book which We explained with knowledge—
phrases.explanation: Allah has brought a Book explained with knowledge. The verse presents the Qur’an as carefully clarified guidance, responding to the claim that people were left without a clear message from their Lord.

phrases.translation: a guide and mercy
phrases.explanation: The Book is described as both a guide and a mercy. It directs believers toward right conduct while offering help from Allah, not merely information about religious ideas or moral direction.

phrases.translation: for those who believe
phrases.explanation: This guidance and mercy are for those who believe. The verse connects the benefit of revelation with a willing response, inviting people to receive the Book rather than turn away from it.

phrases.translation: Do they only await the fulfilment ˹of its warning˺?
phrases.explanation: The verse asks whether the people are waiting for the warning’s fulfilment. It challenges delay, since waiting until consequences become visible may leave no opportunity to respond or avoid the promised judgment.

phrases.translation: The Day it will be fulfilled, those who ignored it before will say, “The messengers of our Lord certainly came with the truth.
phrases.explanation: When the warning is fulfilled, those who ignored it will admit that the messengers came with the truth. Their recognition after the event cannot replace the chance they had to believe earlier.

phrases.translation: Are there any intercessors who can plead on our behalf?
phrases.explanation: They ask whether any intercessors can plead for them. The question shows their search for rescue after judgment, when the false supports they relied on can no longer be trusted.

phrases.translation: Or can we be sent back so we may do ˹good,˺ unlike what we used to do?”
phrases.explanation: They ask whether they can return to do good instead of what they did before. The wish reveals regret, but the opportunity to change belonged to worldly life, not after the warning was fulfilled.

phrases.translation: They will have certainly ruined themselves,
phrases.explanation: They have ruined themselves through their choices. The verse describes the loss as self-caused, rather than the result of an unfair judgment or the failure of a genuine helper, and their own actions.

phrases.translation: and whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them
phrases.explanation: The gods they fabricated will fail them. Their invented objects of worship cannot provide the rescue they hoped for, reinforcing the surah’s call to worship Allah alone in this final scene.

phrases.translation: Indeed your Lord is Allah Who created the heavens and the earth in six Days,
phrases.explanation: Allah created the heavens and earth in six Days. The verse directs attention to the Creator and the ordered creation, without inviting speculation about how divine action should be imagined.

phrases.translation: then established Himself on the Throne.
phrases.explanation: The verse says Allah then established Himself on the Throne. It affirms divine authority over creation while leaving the nature of this description to Allah, rather than comparing it to human bodies or rule.

phrases.translation: He makes the day and night overlap in rapid succession.
phrases.explanation: Day and night overlap in rapid succession. The regular cycle marks time and shapes life on earth, inviting people to notice the order that Allah maintains throughout human life and every generation.

phrases.translation: He created the sun, the moon, and the stars—all subjected by His command.
phrases.explanation: The sun, moon, and stars are subjected by Allah’s command. Their movements are presented as part of an ordered creation, not as independent powers deserving worship or treated as gods.

phrases.translation: The creation and the command belong to Him ˹alone˺.
phrases.explanation: Both creation and command belong to Allah alone. The verse joins the making of the world with authority over it, rejecting the idea that created beings share divine power over all beings.

phrases.translation: Blessed is Allah—Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: Allah is blessed, the Lord of all worlds. The closing calls for reverence and gratitude to the Creator whose power and care extend beyond any single community or place, and invites people to praise Him.

phrases.translation: Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly.
phrases.explanation: People are told to call upon Allah humbly and secretly. The verse values sincerity and reverence in prayer, without requiring people to make their devotion a public display or to seek human praise.

phrases.translation: Surely He does not like the transgressors
phrases.explanation: Allah does not like the transgressors. The warning places limits on conduct and prayer, discouraging arrogance or excess while asking people to approach God with humility and not exceed proper bounds.

phrases.translation: Do not spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order.
phrases.explanation: People must not spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order. The command opposes destructive conduct that damages the conditions needed for communities and life to flourish.

phrases.translation: And call upon Him with hope and fear.
phrases.explanation: Prayer should combine hope and fear. Hope turns people toward Allah’s mercy, while fear keeps them mindful of accountability and guards against treating forgiveness as permission to do wrong in prayer and conduct.

phrases.translation: Indeed, Allah’s mercy is always close to the good-doers
phrases.explanation: Allah’s mercy is close to those who do good. The verse connects moral action with hope in divine compassion and encourages believers to combine prayer with practical goodness through their choices.

phrases.translation: He is the One Who sends the winds ushering in His mercy.
phrases.explanation: Allah sends winds that usher in His mercy. The wind is described through its role in bringing rain, making a familiar feature of weather a sign of provision and care.

phrases.translation: When they bear heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land
phrases.explanation: Heavy clouds are driven to a lifeless land. The verse traces how rain reaches places without visible life, preparing for the growth and fruit described next through processes beyond human command.

phrases.translation: and then cause rain to fall, producing every type of fruit.
phrases.explanation: Rain produces every kind of fruit. The sequence from wind to clouds to harvest shows how nourishment depends on processes people cannot command by themselves and provides for people and other life.

phrases.translation: Similarly, We will bring the dead to life,
phrases.explanation: Allah will similarly bring the dead to life. The revival of dry land becomes an image that helps people understand the possibility of resurrection after death and the renewal of life.

phrases.translation: so perhaps you will be mindful
phrases.explanation: The purpose is that people may be mindful. Observing rain and renewed growth can remind them of Allah’s provision and prepare them to take the promise of resurrection seriously in this life and the next.

phrases.translation: The fertile land produces abundantly by the Will of its Lord,
phrases.explanation: Fertile land produces abundantly by its Lord’s will. The verse recognizes that good conditions contribute to growth, while ultimately placing the outcome within Allah’s permission and care, including soil and setting.

phrases.translation: whereas the infertile land hardly produces anything.
phrases.explanation: Infertile land hardly produces anything. The contrast with fertile soil makes the difference in response visible, even when rain is offered, preparing the analogy about how people receive the signs.

phrases.translation: This is how We vary ˹Our˺ lessons
phrases.explanation: Allah varies His lessons just as the verse contrasts fertile and infertile land. The image invites readers to consider whether they respond to guidance with openness or remain unreceptive to its different forms.

phrases.translation: to those who are thankful
phrases.explanation: The lessons are for those who are thankful. Gratitude helps people recognize the source of provision and respond to revelation, rather than treating both as things owed to them in prayer and action.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We sent Noah to his people.
phrases.explanation: Allah sent Noah to his people as a messenger. The verse begins the account of his mission, showing that guidance came to communities through messengers from among them to guide and warn them.

phrases.translation: He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him.
phrases.explanation: Noah calls his people to worship Allah, saying there is no other god except Him. The message is the same central monotheism repeated throughout the surah and lies at the heart of Noah’s call.

phrases.translation: I truly fear for you the torment of a tremendous Day.”
phrases.explanation: Noah says he fears they will face the torment of a tremendous Day. His warning expresses concern for his people and urges them to turn back before the consequences of rejection arrive.

phrases.translation: But the chiefs of his people said, “We surely see that you are clearly misguided.”
phrases.explanation: The chiefs accuse Noah of being clearly misguided. Their position and influence do not make the accusation true, and the verse introduces the resistance a messenger may face from community leaders.

phrases.translation: He replied, “O my people! I am not misguided!
phrases.explanation: Noah rejects the chiefs’ accusation that he is misguided. His answer calmly distinguishes their judgment of him from the message he carries, introducing the mission he is about to describe.

phrases.translation: But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: Noah says he is a messenger from the Lord of all worlds. He presents his authority as coming from Allah, not from status or personal ambition, and speaks for a universal Creator.

phrases.translation: conveying to you my Lord’s messages
phrases.explanation: Noah conveys the messages entrusted to him by his Lord. His role is to deliver revelation faithfully, rather than adjust it to win approval from the people who challenge him.

phrases.translation: and giving you ˹sincere˺ advice.
phrases.explanation: Noah also gives his people sincere advice. His warning is offered for their benefit, showing that a messenger’s confrontation with wrongdoing can come from concern rather than hostility, even when the advice is unwelcome.

phrases.translation: And I know from Allah what you do not know
phrases.explanation: Noah knows from Allah what his people do not know. The verse points to knowledge received through revelation, including the consequences of choices that his audience may not yet recognize.

phrases.translation: Do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord through one of your own,
phrases.explanation: Noah asks whether it is astonishing that a reminder came through one of the people themselves. A familiar messenger is not a reason to dismiss a message that comes from Allah.

phrases.translation: warning you,
phrases.explanation: The reminder is meant to warn the people. A warning makes danger known before it arrives, giving listeners time to reconsider and avoid the consequences of rejecting guidance before harm comes.

phrases.translation: so you may beware and perhaps be shown mercy?”
phrases.explanation: The purpose is that they may become mindful and receive mercy. The verse presents warning as an opportunity for protection and compassion, not merely a prediction of punishment for the community.

phrases.translation: But they rejected him,
phrases.explanation: Noah’s people reject him despite the warning. Their response sets up the contrast between those who heed the message and those who persist in denying Allah’s signs, despite Noah’s sincerity and concern.

phrases.translation: so We saved him and those with him in the Ark,
phrases.explanation: Allah saves Noah and those with him in the Ark. Their rescue shows that divine mercy protects the believers even when a society around them refuses the messenger and faces the flood.

phrases.translation: and drowned those who rejected Our signs. They were certainly a blind people
phrases.explanation: Those who rejected the signs are drowned and described as a blind people. Blindness here means failure to recognize guidance, not a physical condition or judgment about people with visual disabilities.

phrases.translation: And to the people of ’Âd We sent their brother Hûd.
phrases.explanation: Allah sends Hud to the people of Ad, calling him their brother as a member of their community. The phrase presents the messenger as someone familiar to the people he addresses.

phrases.translation: He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him.
phrases.explanation: Hud calls his people to worship Allah alone, with no other god besides Him. This message of monotheism is central to the prophetic accounts throughout the surah and addresses his own community.

phrases.translation: Will you not then fear Him?”
phrases.explanation: Hud asks whether they will not fear Allah. The question urges them to take divine accountability seriously and to let reverence shape their response to the message and guide their choices.

phrases.translation: The disbelieving chiefs of his people responded, “We surely see you as a fool, and we certainly think you are a liar.”
phrases.explanation: The disbelieving chiefs call Hud a fool and a liar. Their insults reveal rejection rather than engage with his message, showing how community leaders can use status to dismiss a warning.

phrases.translation: Hûd replied, “O my people! I am no fool!
phrases.explanation: Hud rejects the claim that he is foolish. He answers the insult directly, but returns to the substance of his mission rather than responding with a matching personal attack or insulting them back.

phrases.translation: But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds
phrases.explanation: Hud says he is a messenger from the Lord of all worlds. Like Noah, he grounds his authority in Allah and describes a responsibility to convey the message to his people.

phrases.translation: conveying to you my Lord’s messages.
phrases.explanation: Hud conveys the messages of his Lord. His responsibility is to deliver divine guidance, not to claim that the message originates in his own ideas or authority, and to share it with his people.

phrases.translation: And I am your sincere advisor
phrases.explanation: Hud describes himself as a sincere adviser to his people. The claim answers their accusations by emphasizing that he seeks their welfare, even when his advice is unwelcome and challenges their choices for their future.

phrases.translation: Do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord through one of your own so he may warn you?
phrases.explanation: Hud asks whether a reminder through one of their own is astonishing. The messenger’s familiarity should make the warning understandable, not undermine its truth or urgency as guidance from Allah for them.

phrases.translation: Remember that He made you successors after the people of Noah
phrases.explanation: Hud reminds the people of Ad that Allah made them successors after Noah’s people. Their inheritance of the earth is a gift, but also a responsibility that earlier history should teach them to value.

phrases.translation: and increased you greatly in stature.
phrases.explanation: Allah increased the people of Ad greatly in stature. Their strength and presence were blessings, not proof that they were beyond accountability or could ignore the One who gave them these advantages.

phrases.translation: So remember Allah’s favours,
phrases.explanation: Hud urges them to remember Allah’s favours. Gratitude requires recognizing the source of their strength and prosperity, instead of treating these gifts as reasons for pride or claiming them as entitlement.

phrases.translation: so you may be successful.”
phrases.explanation: Remembering the favours may lead them to success. The verse ties gratitude to a better outcome and calls the people to respond before their power is lost and their opportunity has passed.

phrases.translation: They said, “Have you come to us so that we would worship Allah alone and abandon what our forefathers used to worship?
phrases.explanation: The people of Ad object that worshipping Allah alone would require abandoning their forefathers’ practices. Their question shows how attachment to tradition can become resistance to a direct call for monotheism.

phrases.translation: Then bring us what you threaten us with,
phrases.explanation: They demand the punishment Hud warns about. Instead of considering the warning, they challenge him to make it happen, displaying confidence that they can defy its consequences and impatience with his message.

phrases.translation: if what you say is true!”
phrases.explanation: They add that the threat should come if Hud is truthful. Their demand turns a warning into a test, though the truth of the message does not depend on immediate punishment.

phrases.translation: He said, “You will certainly be subjected to your Lord’s torment and wrath.
phrases.explanation: Hud tells the people they will face their Lord’s torment and wrath. The warning answers their challenge by making clear that rejecting guidance has consequences, even if they have not yet arrived.

phrases.translation: Do you dispute with me regarding the so-called gods which you and your forefathers have made up—
phrases.explanation: Hud asks why they dispute over gods invented by themselves and their forefathers. The question exposes the lack of revealed authority behind the objects they worship, rather than offering reasoned proof.

phrases.translation: a practice Allah has never authorized?
phrases.explanation: Allah never authorized the practice, Hud says. The verse challenges his people to distinguish inherited belief from a command actually given by God, and to ask whether revelation supports it.

phrases.translation: Then wait! I too am waiting with you.”
phrases.explanation: Hud tells them to wait, and says that he too is waiting. His words express confidence in Allah’s judgment without attempting to force the people to accept the warning or control their response.

phrases.translation: So We saved him and those with him by Our mercy
phrases.explanation: Allah saves Hud and those with him by His mercy. Their rescue is presented as divine care, while the people who denied the signs face the outcome of their rejection.

phrases.translation: and uprooted those who denied Our signs.
phrases.explanation: Those who denied Allah’s signs are uprooted. The strong image describes the end of the people’s power and refuses to let their former status, homes, or authority appear permanent in history.

phrases.translation: They were not believers
phrases.explanation: They were not believers. The concise ending contrasts the rescued group with those who rejected the message, summarizing the difference in their response to Allah’s signs and the outcome that followed.

phrases.translation: And to the people of Thamûd We sent their brother Ṣâliḥ.
phrases.explanation: Allah sends Salih to the people of Thamud and calls him their brother. As with Noah and Hud, the messenger is from among those he addresses, making the warning familiar to them.

phrases.translation: He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him.
phrases.explanation: Salih calls his people to worship Allah alone. The repeated message of the prophets is not a separate tribal custom but a call to recognize and obey the one Creator.

phrases.translation: A clear proof has come to you from your Lord:
phrases.explanation: Salih says a clear proof has come from their Lord. The verse presents his message as supported by a sign, not merely an unsupported assertion by a person seeking influence.

phrases.translation: this is Allah’s she-camel as a sign to you.
phrases.explanation: The she-camel is identified as a sign from Allah. Its presence gives the people a concrete reminder of the message and a test of whether they will respect the command that follows.

phrases.translation: So leave her to graze ˹freely˺ on Allah’s land and do not harm her,
phrases.explanation: The people are told to let the she-camel graze freely on Allah’s land and not harm her. The command makes respect for the sign part of their response to revelation.

phrases.translation: or else you will be overcome by a painful punishment
phrases.explanation: Harming the she-camel would bring a painful punishment. Salih states the consequence in advance, giving his people a clear choice before they later decide to challenge the command and its warning.

phrases.translation: Remember when He made you successors after ’Âd
phrases.explanation: Salih reminds Thamud that Allah made them successors after Ad. The change of peoples should teach them that strength and a place in history are gifts, not guarantees of permanence.

phrases.translation: and established you in the land—
phrases.explanation: Allah established Thamud in the land. Their security and resources came through divine provision, calling for gratitude rather than arrogance and careful stewardship. The reminder follows their succession after Ad and precedes the description of their homes.

phrases.translation: ˹and˺ you built palaces on its plains
phrases.explanation: The people built palaces on the plains. The verse notes their skill and resources, then contrasts these achievements with the responsibility to remember Allah and avoid corruption, rather than seek comfort alone.

phrases.translation: and carved homes into mountains.
phrases.explanation: They also carved homes into mountains. Their impressive construction demonstrates capacity, but technical skill does not excuse wrongdoing or place a society beyond accountability, even when work required planning and skill.

phrases.translation: So remember Allah’s favours, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.”
phrases.explanation: Salih tells them to remember Allah’s favours and not spread corruption. Gratitude must shape how people use prosperity, so their achievements do not become a means of harming others or the land.

phrases.translation: The arrogant chiefs of his people asked the lowly who believed among them,
phrases.explanation: The arrogant chiefs address the lowly believers among their people. The contrast in status exposes the chiefs’ assumption that social rank should determine whose belief deserves respect or even a hearing.

phrases.translation: “Are you certain that Ṣâliḥ has been sent by his Lord?”
phrases.explanation: They ask whether Salih has truly been sent by his Lord. Their question casts doubt on the messenger while overlooking the substance of the message and the sign he brought.

phrases.translation: They replied,
phrases.explanation: The believers answer the chiefs’ question directly. Their response does not rely on status or wealth, but on their conviction that Salih’s message is true despite the chiefs’ pressure and ridicule.

phrases.translation: “We certainly believe in what he has been sent with.”
phrases.explanation: They say they believe in what Salih was sent with. The verse shows that faith is not limited to the powerful and that a community’s marginalized members may recognize truth its leaders reject.

phrases.translation: The arrogant said,
phrases.explanation: The arrogant chiefs reply to the believers. The verse highlights the sharp difference in how the two groups respond to Salih, despite living in the same community and hearing the same message.

phrases.translation: “We surely reject what you believe in.”
phrases.explanation: The chiefs reject what the believers accept. Their pride and status do not make their rejection sound, and the next verse shows how that refusal becomes open defiance of the message and its truth.

phrases.translation: Then they killed the she-camel—defying their Lord’s command—
phrases.explanation: The people kill the she-camel in defiance of their Lord’s command. The act is not only harm to an animal but a deliberate rejection of the sign and warning Salih gave them.

phrases.translation: and challenged ˹Ṣâliḥ˺, “Bring us what you threaten us with,
phrases.explanation: After killing the camel, they challenge Salih to bring the punishment he warned about. Their words show that the earlier warning did not lead them to reconsider or seek forgiveness.

phrases.translation: if you are ˹truly˺ one of the messengers.”
phrases.explanation: They insist that Salih prove he is a messenger by making the threat come true. Their defiance treats punishment as a spectacle, while the verse has already made their responsibility clear.

phrases.translation: Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them,
phrases.explanation: An overwhelming earthquake strikes the people of Thamud. The sudden event fulfills the warning and ends the confidence with which they had challenged Salih, confirming that his warning was not empty.

phrases.translation: and they fell lifeless in their homes
phrases.explanation: They fall lifeless in their homes. The verse shows that their buildings and former security could not protect them from the consequence of rejecting the sign and command, even with strong homes and defenses.

phrases.translation: So he turned away from them, saying,
phrases.explanation: Salih turns away from his people and speaks to them. His departure follows their rejection, but he still reminds them one last time of the message and advice he had already delivered.

phrases.translation: “O my people! Surely I conveyed to you my Lord’s message and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice,
phrases.explanation: Salih says he conveyed his Lord’s message and gave sincere advice. He affirms that his responsibility was to communicate faithfully and counsel them, even though they chose not to listen.

phrases.translation: but you do not like ˹sincere˺ advisors.”
phrases.explanation: The people did not like sincere advisers. The final words explain their rejection as a refusal of unwelcome counsel, warning that people may resist guidance precisely because it asks them to change.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when Lot scolded ˹the men of˺ his people, ˹saying,˺ “Do you commit a shameful deed that no man has ever done before
phrases.explanation: The account turns to Lot, who rebukes the men of his people for a shameful deed. The verse begins a warning about conduct the text describes as unprecedented, and the next verse continues his words.

phrases.translation: You lust after men instead of women! You are certainly transgressors.”
phrases.explanation: Lot rebukes his people for pursuing men instead of women and calls their conduct transgression. The verse records his moral warning in this specific narrative, not permission for people to demean or harm others.

phrases.translation: But his people’s only response was to say,
phrases.explanation: Lot’s people respond with a demand to expel him and those with him. Rather than answer his warning, they try to remove the people whose conduct and message challenge their own.

phrases.translation: “Expel them from your land! They are a people who wish to remain chaste!”
phrases.explanation: They mock Lot’s followers for wishing to remain chaste. The reply turns a moral concern into an insult and shows the community using ridicule to justify expelling those who disagree.

phrases.translation: So We saved him and his family
phrases.explanation: Allah saves Lot and his family from the punishment that follows. The rescue distinguishes those who were protected from the surrounding people who continued to reject the warning and its consequences.

phrases.translation: except his wife,
phrases.explanation: Lot’s wife is excepted from the family saved. The verse presents her as among the doomed, showing that family connection alone does not determine a person’s response, moral choices, or outcome.

phrases.translation: who was one of the doomed
phrases.explanation: She is described as one of the doomed. The account places the consequence on her own position in the story, not on every member of a family or every spouse of a messenger.

phrases.translation: We poured upon them a rain ˹of brimstone˺.
phrases.explanation: A rain of brimstone is poured upon Lot’s people. The verse describes the punishment that follows their rejection, bringing the warning to a sudden and devastating end in the story.

phrases.translation: See what was the end of the wicked
phrases.explanation: The audience is asked to consider the end of the wicked. The reminder invites reflection on the outcome of persistent wrongdoing rather than fascination with destruction itself or celebration of suffering.

phrases.translation: And to the people of Midian We sent their brother Shu’aib.
phrases.explanation: Allah sends Shu’aib to the people of Midian and calls him their brother. Like earlier messengers in the surah, he is familiar to the people he addresses and comes to warn them.

phrases.translation: He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him.
phrases.explanation: Shu’aib calls his people to worship Allah alone. The verse places monotheism at the center of his message before turning to the economic conduct that is harming the community and its members.

phrases.translation: A clear proof has already come to you from your Lord.
phrases.explanation: Shu’aib says a clear proof has come from their Lord. His call is presented as supported by revelation, not simply by his personal view of how society should behave or conduct itself.

phrases.translation: So give just measure and weight,
phrases.explanation: The people are told to give just measure and weight. Honest measurement protects buyers and sellers alike, making fairness in ordinary trade part of religious responsibility and a means of protecting trust.

phrases.translation: do not defraud people of their property,
